creator: Alexander Terp
description:
a_2Ky2ptlug names two directions for the shared devenv container and settles on neither. Two parallel rounds have now paid for that, and the evidence is worth attaching before somebody chooses.

## Round 1, 2026-09-06

The collision was avoided by hand. The integrator read a_2Ky2ptlug while scoping the round and told three of four slots not to touch docker at all, so only one could ever use --ssh or --corpus-linux. That is a real cost: it is a whole tier removed from three slots for a reason that has nothing to do with their work, decided by an integrator who happened to have read the card.

## Round 2, same day

The one slot that *was* cleared still lost time. The container had been up 16 hours holding a different worktree ssh key, so --corpus-linux failed at publickey with nothing on either side saying the image had been built around somebody else key. Recovery was devenv down and up, which rebuilds the shared image around the current worktree - re-arming the same trap for whoever runs it next.

So the workaround does not survive contact with parallel work. Serializing by hand still leaves the loser broken, because the breakage is baked into an image rather than held by a running process, and nothing checks it.

## What this suggests, without deciding it

a_2Ky2ptlug two directions were: derive image, container and port from the worktree so each gets its own; or keep one container and stop the key being per-worktree.

Round 2 adds a cheap third that is not exclusive with either: whatever the container is, it should say whose key it holds and refuse rather than fail at publickey. A tier that fails with "this image was built for muster-3" costs a reader nothing; one that fails with "Permission denied (publickey)" costs them the twenty minutes it cost here.
title: The devenv key collision cost a second round, and the decision is still open
